clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive N-linked congenital disorder of glycosylation caused by ALG1 mutations
One of the more common of the rare type I CDGs after PMM2-CDG
Typically presents with a severe multisystem phenotype: developmental delay, epilepsy, hypotonia and microcephaly
Frequent additional features include coagulopathy, nephrotic-range protein loss, immune dysfunction and dysmorphism
Transferrin isoform analysis (isoelectric focusing) shows a type I pattern, prompting confirmatory genetics
There is no curative therapy; management is supportive and multidisciplinary
Severe neonatal-onset disease often has a poor prognosis
reference.pathophysiology: ALG1 encodes a mannosyltransferase that acts early in the assembly of the lipid-linked oligosaccharide precursor used for N-linked glycosylation in the endoplasmic reticulum. Deficient activity impairs building of the dolichol-linked glycan, so many secreted and membrane glycoproteins are under-glycosylated. Because N-glycosylation is required for the correct folding, stability and function of numerous proteins (including clotting factors, hormones and immune proteins), the defect produces a multisystem disorder with prominent neurological involvement, coagulopathy and protein-losing features, as seen across the type I CDGs.
additionalDifferentials: PMM2-CDG and other type I congenital disorders of glycosylation
Congenital nephrotic syndrome of other cause
additionalInvestigations: Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing or mass spectrometry (type I pattern)
Coagulation studies (including factors affected by glycosylation)
Assessment of renal protein loss and immune function
redFlags: Unexplained coagulopathy with bleeding or thrombosis
reference.prognosis: The prognosis is variable but often poor in early-onset multisystem disease, with significant early mortality; milder phenotypes with longer survival and predominant neurological impairment occur.
pitfalls: Not sending transferrin glycoform analysis in an unexplained multisystem infantile disorder
Attributing coagulopathy to liver disease rather than glycosylation defect
Overlooking CDG in a child labelled as having a non-specific epileptic encephalopathy
Assuming a normal transferrin screen fully excludes all CDGs
references: Textbook of Inborn Metabolic Diseases (standard reference)
management: No curative treatment is available; care is supportive and multidisciplinary through a metabolic centre
Manage epilepsy with anticonvulsants and provide developmental therapy for hypotonia and delay
Correct coagulation abnormalities peri-operatively and during illness given glycosylation-dependent clotting factor deficiency
Nutritional support and management of nephrotic-range protein loss and associated oedema
Immune assessment with treatment of infections and immunoglobulin support where dysfunction is significant
Regular neurodevelopmental, feeding and growth review
Genetic counselling and family screening for this autosomal recessive disorder
